The findings reveal that AI disproportionately benefits highly educated workers while increasing employment vulnerability among medium-skilled workers, thereby reinforcing labor market polarization. Moreover, innovation significantly moderates these effects by transforming AI-driven productivity gains into new employment opportunities. The study contributes to the literature by demonstrating that innovation conditions the employment effects of AI rather than acting solely as an independent growth factor.

Following previous studies on technological change and employment (Acemoglu & Restrepo, 2020; Aghion et al., 2021), the analysis distinguishes employment outcomes according to three educational groups based on the International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED): low educational attainment (ISCED 0–2), medium educational attainment (ISCED 3–4), and tertiary education (ISCED 5–8).
